quests.passageTopic: Opinion: The Case for a Shorter Week
quests.passage: Last year, our council tested a four-day working week for its office staff, with no reduction in pay. The results were striking: sick days fell by a quarter, and the number of resident complaints answered within 48 hours rose from 71 percent to 86 percent. Critics argue that other employers could not afford the same experiment, but that misses the point. Productivity does not rise because people work fewer hours; it rises because they stop wasting the hours they have. Any manager who has sat through a pointless Friday afternoon meeting knows this to be true. It is time other employers followed the council's lead.

quests.passage: Dear Mr. Fraser, thank you for your letter of 9 May regarding flight BX204. We are sorry that your flight was cancelled at short notice and that you spent six hours at the airport trying to find another one. Under the airline's policy, passengers whose flights are cancelled less than 14 days before departure are entitled to a refund or a seat on the next available flight; compensation is paid only when the cancellation is caused by something within the airline's control. Our records show that your flight was cancelled because a storm closed the airport, which we classify as outside our control. We have therefore refunded your ticket in full but are unable to offer further compensation. We hope to welcome you on board again.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Quiet Table
quests.passage: Ms. Haddad had eaten lunch at the same corner table for eleven years, and Joel, the waiter, knew her order without asking: a bowl of mushroom soup and black tea. Today she arrived at twelve, as always, but she sat with her coat on and left the menu closed. Joel brought the soup anyway. She thanked him, looked at it, and pushed it gently aside. "Everything all right?" he asked. She smiled in a way that did not reach her eyes. "My husband's birthday," she said. "He always ordered the fish." Joel nodded, took the soup away, and came back with a plate of grilled fish, which he set down without a word.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Book Review: The Salt Road
quests.passage: Nora Vance's account of traveling the old salt trade routes is easy to admire and, at times, frustrating to read. Her descriptions of the desert towns are vivid enough that I found myself checking my own water bottle, and the chapter on the caravan guides is a small masterpiece. Yet the book keeps promising an argument it never delivers. Vance hints repeatedly that the salt trade shaped the region's politics, then retreats into anecdote each time she approaches the point. Readers who enjoy atmosphere will be rewarded; those hoping for analysis will close the final page feeling short-changed.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Night Train to Inverness
quests.passage: There is no faster way to reach the Highlands than flying, but there is hardly a better one than the sleeper train. It leaves London at 9:15 p.m., and by the time passengers have eaten in the lounge car and negotiated their narrow bunks, the lights of the suburbs have gone. The ride is not silent; the carriages creak and the corridor doors bang. Yet I slept better than I do in most hotels, and woke to sheep-dotted hills in the pale morning. The train arrives at 10:30 a.m., about three hours later than a flight would, and costs a third less than the cheapest air fare. For anyone not in a hurry, it is the obvious choice.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Woman Who Mapped the River
quests.passageTopic: The Woman Who Mapped the River
quests.passage: In 1921, Edith Marsh was hired as a clerk by the river authority, a job that involved filing survey reports. Within a year she noticed that two reports describing the same bend in the river disagreed by several hundred meters. Instead of ignoring the error, she spent her evenings comparing every report in the archive, and eventually produced a single corrected map. Her supervisors, who had not asked for it, were at first irritated by the extra work it created for the surveyors. But when floods hit the valley in 1927, it was Marsh's map that the engineers used to decide which villages to evacuate, and far fewer homes were lost than feared.
